claim: Cancer cell metabolism is heavily influenced by microenvironmental factors, including nutrient availability.
source: Cancer cell metabolism is heavily influenced by microenvironmental factors, including nutrient availability.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: The study utilized quantitative metabolomics methods to measure the absolute concentrations of >118 metabolites in plasma and tumor interstitial fluid.
source: To measure the extracellular nutrient levels available to tumors, we utilized quantitative metabolomics methods to measure the absolute concentrations of >118 metabolites in plasma and tumor interstitial fluid, the extracellular fluid that perfuses tumors.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the methodology used to measure metabolites.

claim: The nutrients available to tumors differ from those present in circulation.
source: Comparison of nutrient levels in tumor interstitial fluid and plasma revealed that the nutrients available to tumors differ from those present in circulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tumor type affects local nutrient availability.
source: Further, by comparing interstitial fluid nutrient levels between autochthonous and transplant models of murine pancreatic and lung adenocarcinoma, we found that tumor type, anatomical location and animal diet affect local nutrient availability.
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by comparative analysis of different tumor models.

claim: Anatomical location affects local nutrient availability.
source: Further, by comparing interstitial fluid nutrient levels between autochthonous and transplant models of murine pancreatic and lung adenocarcinoma, we found that tumor type, anatomical location and animal diet affect local nutrient availability.
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract and supported by comparative analysis of different tumor models.

claim: Animal limbs transformed with oncogenic viruses exhibit increased glucose uptake and lactate secretion relative to unaffected limbs.
source: For example, animal limbs transformed with oncogenic viruses exhibit increased glucose uptake and lactate secretion relative to unaffected limbs (Cori and Cori, 1925).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to historical work by Cori and Cori, 1925.

claim: Some aspects of tumor metabolism, including higher rates of glucose fermentation to lactate, are cell-intrinsic features that are retained when cancer cells are isolated from tumors.
source: Some aspects of tumor metabolism, including higher rates of glucose fermentation to lactate, are cell-intrinsic features that are retained when cancer cells are isolated from tumors (Koppenol et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koppenol et al., 2011.

claim: Oncogenic lesions or epigenetic state alter cellular metabolism, causing phenotypes such as increased glycolysis.
source: Indeed, numerous studies have delineated how cell-intrinsic factors such as oncogenic lesions or epigenetic state alter cellular metabolism, causing phenotypes such as increased glycolysis (Nagarajan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nagarajan et al., 2016.

claim: Tumors have modified tissue architecture and an altered tissue microenvironment that can impact the metabolism of tumors.
source: However, beyond cell-intrinsic alterations, tumors have modified tissue architecture and an altered tissue microenvironment; these cell-extrinsic factors can also impact the metabolism of tumors (Muir et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Muir et al., 2018.

claim: The metabolic utilization of both glucose and the amino acid glutamine differs between cells growing in culture and murine tumor models.
source: For instance, the metabolic utilization of both glucose and the amino acid glutamine differs between cells growing in culture and murine tumor models (Davidson et al., 2016; Muir et al., 2017; Sellers et al., 2015; Tardito et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Davidson et al., 2016; Muir et al., 2017; Sellers et al., 2015; Tardito et al., 2015.

claim: The metabolic enzymes that cancer cells rely upon for proliferation in culture are different than those that the same cells utilize to support growth and survival in tumors.
source: Further, the metabolic enzymes that cancer cells rely upon for proliferation in culture are different than those that the same cells utilize to support growth and survival in tumors (Alvarez et al., 2017; Possemato et al., 2011; Yau et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alvarez et al., 2017; Possemato et al., 2011; Yau et al., 2017.

claim: Environmental nutrient availability is an important regulator of cancer cell metabolism.
source: In particular, environmental nutrient availability is an important regulator of cancer cell metabolism (Cantor et al., 2017; Muir et al., 2017; Schug et al., 2015; Tardito et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cantor et al., 2017; Muir et al., 2017; Schug et al., 2015; Tardito et al., 2015.

claim: Nutrient differences between standard cell culture and animal tumor models can drive substantial changes in cancer cell metabolism that alter the response of cancer cells to metabolically targeted drugs.
source: Nutrient differences between standard cell culture and animal tumor models can drive substantial changes in cancer cell metabolism that alter the response of cancer cells to metabolically targeted drugs (Cantor et al., 2017; Gui et al., 2016; Muir et al., 2017; Palm et al., 2015), such that drugs that inhibit proliferation of cancer cells in culture fail to exhibit efficacy in tumors derived from the same cells (Biancur et al., 2017; Davidson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cantor et al., 2017; Gui et al., 2016; Muir et al., 2017; Palm et al., 2015; Biancur et al., 2017; Davidson et al., 2016.

claim: Interstitial fluid perfuses through the tissue or tumor, exchanging nutrients and wastes with cells.
source: The interstitial fluid (IF) then perfuses through the tissue or tumor, exchanging nutrients and wastes with cells.
evidence: This is a description of the physiological role of interstitial fluid based on established knowledge.

claim: The IF glucose concentration in healthy skin is very similar to that of circulating plasma.
source: Indeed, the IF glucose concentration in healthy skin is very similar to that of circulating plasma (Lönnroth et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lönnroth et al., 1987.

claim: Tumors commonly have an abnormal vasculature with few vessels transporting blood.
source: In contrast to the functional vessels found in normal tissues, tumors commonly have an abnormal vasculature with few vessels transporting blood (Fukumura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fukumura et al., 2010.

claim: Glucose levels in the TIF of some tumors are lower than in the circulation, while lactate levels are higher.
source: Indeed glucose levels in the TIF of some tumors are lower than in the circulation, while lactate levels are higher (Burgess and Sylven, 1962; Gullino et al., 1964; Ho et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burgess and Sylven, 1962; Gullino et al., 1964; Ho et al., 2015.

claim: The centrifugation method does not cause lysis of cells when performed on human tumor samples.
source: Critically, this centrifugation method does not cause lysis of cells when performed on human tumor samples, ensuring that the isolated fluid is interstitial and not intracellular fluid (Haslene-Hox et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haslene-Hox et al., 2011.

claim: The LDH activity in the entire TIF volume is <1% of LDH activity found in the tumor.
source: By measuring LDH activity (an intracellular enzyme and marker of intracellular fluid) in KP-/-C tumor, plasma, and TIF samples, we determined that the LDH activity in the entire TIF volume is <1% of LDH activity found in the tumor (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Levels of LDH activity in the PDAC TIF samples were ~20 fold higher than those found in plasma samples.
source: Though levels of LDH activity in the PDAC TIF samples were ~20 fold higher than those found in plasma samples, similar or higher LDH activities were recovered in TIF of solid tumors isolated by orthogonal methods (~60–80 fold higher LDH activity in TIF than plasma) (Burgess and Sylven, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to literature (Burgess and Sylven, 1962).

claim: TIF isolation by centrifugation does not result in gross cell lysis and intracellular fluid is not a major component of PDAC TIF.
source: These data further confirm that TIF isolation by centrifugation does not result in gross cell lysis and that intracellular fluid is not a major component of PDAC TIF.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the LDH activity measurements.

claim: Principle component analysis did not lead to separate clustering of immediately frozen or TIF-isolated samples.
source: Principle component analysis did not lead to separate clustering of immediately frozen or TIF-isolated samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No increase in succinate and only modest increases in xanthine and hypoxanthine levels were found in tumors samples subjected to TIF isolation.
source: We found no increase in succinate and only modest increases in xanthine and hypoxanthine levels in tumors samples subjected to TIF isolation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D), and the changes observed in xanthine and hypoxanthine were much less than those observed in ischemic tissues (Chouchani et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D and comparison to Chouchani et al., 2014.

claim: The TIF isolation method used does not cause substantial changes in intratumoral metabolite levels.
source: These data suggest that the TIF isolation method used does not cause substantial changes in intratumoral metabolite levels; however, development of faster TIF isolation methods will be required to rigorously evaluate the extent to which the metabolite composition of TIF is altered by the time needed to isolate this fluid.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the metabolite stability data, with acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: 70 metabolites were quantitated using stable isotope dilution.
source: Quantification of these 13C labeled metabolites allowed them to be used as internal standards for absolute quantification of metabolites by stable isotope dilution (Figure 1C). This enabled quantification of 70 metabolites, with the remaining 79 being quantified by external calibration using the library of chemical standards (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the quantification approach.

claim: 79 metabolites were quantified by external calibration using the library of chemical standards.
source: This enabled quantification of 70 metabolites, with the remaining 79 being quantified by external calibration using the library of chemical standards (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the quantification approach.

claim: When the same amounts of 13C stable isotope labeled metabolites were added to water or mouse plasma, detected levels of these 13C standards varied widely depending on whether the metabolites were dissolved in water or plasma.
source: Indeed, when the same amounts of 13C stable isotope labeled metabolites were added to water or mouse plasma, detected levels of these 13C standards varied widely depending on whether the metabolites were dissolved in water or plasma (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Matrix effects alter the ionization and detection of metabolites in different sample types.
source: Absolute LC/MS quantification of metabolites in biological samples such as plasma and TIF is complicated by matrix effects, which alter the ionization and detection of metabolites in different sample types (Trufelli et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trufelli et al., 2011.

claim: Both 12C and 13C metabolites are subject to the same sample-dependent ion enhancement or suppression effects, so quantification by stable isotope dilution does not suffer from systematic errors.
source: However, both 12C and 13C metabolites are subject to the same sample-dependent ion enhancement or suppression effects, so quantification by stable isotope dilution does not suffer from these potential systematic errors (Trufelli et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Trufelli et al., 2011.

claim: Between 118–136 metabolites were measured in individual experiments analyzing plasma and TIF with high levels of inter-day reproducibility.
source: By either isotope dilution or external calibration, we measured between 118–136 metabolites in individual experiments analyzing plasma and TIF with high levels of inter-day reproducibility (stable isotope dilution: Pearson r = 0.9536, p<0.0001; external standard calibration: Pearson r = 0.9516, p<0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Methods of blood collection that require anesthesia can alter circulating metabolite levels.
source: Methods of blood collection that require anesthesia can alter circulating metabolite levels (Overmyer et al., 2015) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Overmyer et al., 2015 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PDAC TIF samples clustered separately from the plasma samples, suggesting that the metabolic composition of PDAC TIF differs from that of plasma.
source: PDAC TIF and plasma samples were profiled using the described metabolomics techniques and grouped by either hierarchical clustering (Figure 2A) or principal component analysis (Figure 2B) of metabolite concentrations. By each method, the PDAC TIF samples clustered separately from the plasma samples, suggesting that the metabolic composition of PDAC TIF differs from that of plasma.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: There was substantial heterogeneity in plasma metabolite concentrations between animals.
source: Interestingly, there was substantial heterogeneity in plasma metabolite concentrations between animals.
evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis.

claim: Heterogeneity in plasma metabolites might arise from differences in feed/fast cycle upon harvesting or circadian fluctuations in circulating metabolites.
source: Plasma and TIF was not harvested from mice at a fixed time, and this heterogeneity in plasma metabolites might arise from differences in feed/fast cycle upon harvesting (Sullivan et al., 2019) or circadian fluctuations in circulating metabolites (Abbondante et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Sullivan et al., 2019 and Abbondante et al., 2016.

claim: PDAC TIF and plasma exhibit different matrix effects.
source: PDAC TIF and plasma exhibit different matrix effects (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which could contribute to the observed global differences in metabolite levels between TIF and plasma.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: PDAC TIF is substantially different from plasma when analysis is limited to only metabolites quantitated using isotopically labeled internal standards.
source: Therefore, we also conducted a comparison of PDAC TIF and plasma metabolite levels using only metabolites quantified by stable isotope dilution. PDAC TIF is still substantially different from plasma when analysis is limited to only metabolites quantitated using isotopically labeled internal standards (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), suggesting that the global metabolite composition of TIF differs from that of plasma.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Glucose was depleted in TIF compared to plasma.
source: Consistent with the avid consumption of glucose observed in tumors and cancer cell lines, glucose was depleted in TIF compared to plasma (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Amino acids known to be produced by tumors such as glycine and glutamate were enriched in TIF.
source: Amino acids known to be produced by tumors such as glycine and glutamate (Hosios et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2012) were enriched in TIF (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and citations to Hosios et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2012.

claim: The amino acid glutamine was present at similar concentrations in TIF and plasma.
source: Interestingly, the amino acid glutamine, which is consumed rapidly by cultured cells (Eagle, 1955; Hosios et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2012), was present at similar concentrations in TIF and plasma (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2E, and citations to Eagle, 1955; Hosios et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2012.

claim: Alanine was abundantly present in both TIF and plasma.
source: We also found that alanine, an amino acid reported to support PDAC cells (Sousa et al., 2016), was abundantly present in both TIF and plasma (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and a citation to Sousa et al., 2016.

claim: Metabolites important for immune cell function such as arginine, tryptophan and cystine were depleted in PDAC TIF compared to plasma.
source: Further, metabolites important for immune cell function such as arginine, tryptophan and cystine (Geiger et al., 2016; Moffett and Namboodiri, 2003; Srivastava et al., 2010) were depleted in PDAC TIF compared to plasma (Figure 2C,G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2C, 2G, 2H, and 2I, and citations to Geiger et al., 2016; Moffett and Namboodiri, 2003; Srivastava et al., 2010.

claim: Levels of ornithine in PDAC TIF increased relative to plasma, suggesting that local arginase activity may account for PDAC depletion of arginine.
source: Additionally, levels of ornithine in PDAC TIF increased relative to plasma, suggesting that local arginase activity (Caldwell et al., 2018) may account for PDAC depletion of arginine (Figure 2J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2J and a citation to Caldwell et al., 2018. The suggestion is an inference from the data.

claim: Many metabolites were enriched in TIF, suggesting that the PDAC tumor microenvironment is not depleted for all nutrients.
source: Many metabolites were enriched in TIF (Figure 2C), suggesting that the PDAC tumor microenvironment is not depleted for all nutrients.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and is an inference from the data.

claim: Tumor size does not appear to dictate PDAC TIF metabolite levels, at least within the size range of tumors tested.
source: We found that, at least within this size range of tumors, tumor size does not appear to dictate PDAC TIF metabolite levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing TIF from large and small PDAC tumors.

claim: PDAC TIF was metabolically distinct from TIF derived from isogenic subcutaneous tumors.
source: Based on measurement of 123 quantitated metabolites that were detectable and quantifiable in this experiment, PDAC TIF was metabolically distinct from TIF derived from isogenic subcutaneous tumors both by principal component analysis (Figure 3B) and by hierarchical clustering (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: Concentrations of tryptophan, arginine and cystine, which are depleted in autochthonous PDAC TIF, were relatively higher in subcutaneous PDAC TIF.
source: Interestingly, concentrations of tryptophan, arginine and cystine, which are depleted in autochthonous PDAC TIF, were relatively higher in subcutaneous PDAC TIF (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3D, 3E, and 3F.

claim: Subcutaneous models of PDAC may not mimic the metabolic microenvironment of PDAC tumors.
source: This suggests that subcutaneous models of PDAC may not mimic the metabolic microenvironment of PDAC tumors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differences in TIF composition between autochthonous and subcutaneous PDAC tumors.

claim: The metabolic composition of TIF is not only determined by tumor-intrinsic factors, but potentially also by the anatomical location in which the tumor is growing.
source: Furthermore, while potentially confounded by comparing transplant and autochthonous PDAC models, these results suggest that the metabolic composition of TIF is not only determined by tumor-intrinsic factors, but potentially also by the anatomical location in which the tumor is growing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differences in TIF composition between autochthonous and subcutaneous PDAC tumors, with acknowledgment of potential confounding factors.

claim: TIF from mice fed standard chow differed from TIF from mice fed a defined diet.
source: Based on measurement of 123 metabolites that were detectable and quantifiable in this experiment, TIF from mice fed standard chow differed from TIF from mice fed a defined diet based on principal component analysis (Figure 4B) and hierarchical clustering (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: There is a strong correlation between TIF to plasma ratio of metabolite concentrations between mice on different diets.
source: Indeed, there is a strong correlation (Pearson r = 0.8927, p<0.0001) between TIF to plasma ratio of metabolite concentrations between mice on different diets (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Linear regression of TIF to plasma ratios in mice fed different diets nearly yields an identity function.
source: Furthermore, linear regression of TIF to plasma ratios in mice fed different diets nearly yields an identity function (slope = 0.9511, R2 = 0.7969) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Dietary perturbation does not broadly affect the scaling factor between TIF and plasma metabolite levels.
source: Thus, while individual TIF metabolite levels are scaled by some factor relative to plasma levels, dietary perturbation does not broadly affect this scaling factor.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis of TIF to plasma ratios across diets.

claim: Systemic metabolic changes can affect the composition of TIF by altering circulating nutrient levels.
source: Thus, in addition to local microenvironmental factors, systemic metabolic changes can affect the composition of TIF by altering circulating nutrient levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dietary intervention experiments.

claim: TIF from subcutaneous tumors derived from LUAD clustered separately from PDAC subcutaneous allograft TIF.
source: Based on measurement of 104 metabolites that were detectable and quantifiable in this experiment, TIF from subcutaneous tumors derived from LUAD clustered separately from PDAC subcutaneous allograft TIF by principal component analysis (Figure 5B) and hierarchical clustering (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Levels of branched-chain amino acids and their catabolites were different between LUAD and PDAC tumors.
source: LUAD and PDAC tumors are known to have different branched-chain amino acid metabolism (Mayers et al., 2016), and levels of branched-chain amino acids and their catabolites were different between LUAD and PDAC tumors (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and a citation to Mayers et al., 2016.

claim: A number of metabolites involved in thiol metabolism are altered between LUAD and PDAC tumors, suggesting potential differences in sulfur metabolism between these tumors.
source: Additionally, a number of metabolites involved in thiol metabolism are altered between LUAD and PDAC tumors (Figure 5D) (Gall et al., 2010; Irino et al., 2016), suggesting potential differences in sulfur metabolism between these tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and citations to Gall et al., 2010; Irino et al., 2016. The suggestion is an inference from the data.

claim: Tissue of origin is a determinant of the metabolic composition of TIF.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that tissue of origin is a determinant of the metabolic composition of TIF.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing TIF from LUAD and PDAC subcutaneous tumors.

claim: TIF samples did not cluster separately based on Keap1 status by principal component analysis.
source: Based on measurement of 131 metabolites that were detectable and quantifiable in this experiment, TIF samples did not cluster separately based on Keap1 status by principal component analysis (Figure 6B), although they could be separated by hierarchical clustering (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Anticipated changes in TIF composition based on alterations to cancer cell metabolism by Keap1 loss, such as decreased glutamine, glucose and cystine, and increased glutamate and lactate, were not observed between TIF samples of Keap1 wild-type and Keap1 null tumors.
source: Surprisingly, anticipated changes in TIF composition based on alterations to cancer cell metabolism by Keap1 loss, such as decreased glutamine, glucose and cystine, and increased glutamate and lactate (Romero et al., 2017) were not observed between TIF samples of Keap1 wild-type and Keap1 null tumors (Figure 6D–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 6D-H and a citation to Romero et al., 2017.

claim: Genetic Keap1 status has less of an effect on metabolic TIF content in subcutaneous lung cancer allografts.
source: Together, these results suggest that genetic Keap1 status has less of an effect on metabolic TIF content in subcutaneous lung cancer allografts, and that not all cancer cell-intrinsic perturbations of metabolism cause detectable changes to the tumor nutrient milieu.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Keap1 loss experiment.

claim: TIF metabolite levels in the murine cancer models assessed are different from the nutrient levels in plasma.
source: We find that TIF metabolite levels in the murine cancer models assessed are different from the nutrient levels in plasma.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding from the study.

claim: Not all nutrients are depleted in TIF, with levels of some being higher than what is found in circulation.
source: Contrary to many assumptions, not all nutrients are depleted in TIF, with levels of some being higher than what is found in circulation.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the metabolite measurements.

claim: Tumors with abnormal vasculature exist largely as a separate compartment from the bulk circulation, and can have different steady state metabolic microenvironments.
source: Thus, our measurements of plasma and TIF nutrient composition are consistent with a model where tumors with abnormal vasculature exist largely as a separate compartment from the bulk circulation, and can have different steady state metabolic microenvironments.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of tumor physiology.

claim: Anti-VEGF therapies are thought to normalize tumor vasculature leading to decreased interstitial pressure and increased perfusion.
source: For example, anti-VEGF therapies are thought to normalize tumor vasculature leading to decreased interstitial pressure and increased perfusion (Jain, 2001), and a number of approaches have been developed to limit the stromal compression of tumor blood vessels that increases tumor pressure and decreases tumor perfusion (Olive et al., 2009; Pinter and Jain, 2017; Provenzano et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jain, 2001; Olive et al., 2009; Pinter and Jain, 2017; Provenzano et al., 2012.

claim: The tumor may contain a population of sub-compartments with different perfusion rates and heterogeneous TIF compositions.
source: While we have considered the tumor as a single compartment and analyzed bulk TIF from the entire tumor, it is possible that the tumor contains a population of sub-compartments with different perfusion rates (Hensley et al., 2016) and heterogeneous TIF compositions (Wagner and Wiig, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Hensley et al., 2016 and Wagner and Wiig, 2015.

claim: Measurements of intratumor metabolites in subsections of tumors suggests that some tumor regions experience different nutrient levels than others.
source: Measurements of intratumor metabolites in subsections of tumors suggests that some tumor regions experience different nutrient levels than others (Pan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 2016.

claim: Perturbations to systemic nutrient levels by altering diet affect TIF composition.
source: Though TIF appears to constitute a separate compartment from plasma, tumor nutrients are ultimately delivered from the circulation. Thus, perturbations to systemic nutrient levels by altering diet affect TIF composition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dietary intervention experiments.

claim: A major mechanism by which diet influences tumor nutrient availability is by altering nutrients available in the circulation.
source: This relationship between plasma and TIF nutrient levels across different diets suggests that TIF levels of metabolites are derived from plasma metabolite concentrations, and changes in plasma metabolite levels lead to scaled changes in TIF metabolite levels. This argues that a major mechanism by which diet influences tumor nutrient availability is by altering nutrients available in the circulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between TIF and plasma metabolite levels across diets.

claim: Subcutaneous models of PDAC may not fully recapitulate the metabolic microenvironment of this disease.
source: This suggests that subcutaneous models of PDAC may not fully recapitulate the metabolic microenvironment of this disease, and is in line with observations that subcutaneous models of PDAC fail to recapitulate many aspects of PDAC tumors including marked stromal infiltration and extracellular matrix deposition (Hwang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Hwang et al., 2016.

claim: Subcutaneous models do not recapitulate all metabolic aspects of the disease.
source: These observations, along with recent findings that subcutaneous PDAC models do not recapitulate whole body metabolic perturbations observed in autochthonous PDAC models and patients (Danai et al., 2018), suggest subcutaneous models do not recapitulate all metabolic aspects of the disease.
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Danai et al., 2018.

claim: Autochthonous PDAC tumors have lower levels of arginine, tryptophan and cystine compared to subcutaneous tumors.
source: Nevertheless, it is intriguing that autochthonous PDAC tumors have lower levels of arginine, tryptophan and cystine compared to subcutaneous tumors.
evidence: This is a summary of the data comparing autochthonous and subcutaneous PDAC TIF.

claim: Stromal myeloid derived cells have been implicated in depleting arginine, tryptophan, and cystine from the tumor microenvironment.
source: Stromal myeloid derived cells have been implicated in depleting each of these nutrients from the tumor microenvironment (Kumar et al., 2016), and murine PDAC tumors are known to contain a large number of myeloid lineage cells (Bayne et al., 2012; Goedegebuure et al., 2011; Stromnes et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kumar et al., 2016; Bayne et al., 2012; Goedegebuure et al., 2011; Stromnes et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2009.

claim: Subcutaneous PDAC tumors are known to have fewer stromal cells.
source: Additionally, subcutaneous PDAC tumors are known to have fewer stromal cells (Hwang et al., 2016; Sousa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hwang et al., 2016; Sousa et al., 2016.

claim: Differences in TIF composition between autochthonous and subcutaneous PDAC tumors could be driven by differences in stromal cell populations between anatomical sites.
source: Thus, it is tempting to speculate that differences in TIF composition between autochthonous and subcutaneous PDAC tumors, including differences in arginine, tryptophan and cystine levels, could be driven by differences in stromal cell populations between anatomical sites.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data and literature.

claim: Factors beyond cancer cell-intrinsic metabolism can be dominant in setting nutrient levels in the microenvironment.
source: Surprisingly, we found no substantial differences in TIF composition between tumors formed from otherwise isogenic LUAD cell lines that differed only in Keap1 loss. These data argue that factors beyond cancer cell-intrinsic metabolism can be dominant in setting nutrient levels in the microenvironment, although future studies are required to determine how other oncogenic alterations alter TIF composition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Keap1 loss experiment.

claim: Differences in metabolite concentrations between TIF and plasma cannot be used to extrapolate consumption and release of metabolites by tumors.
source: However, wild type and Keap1 null cancer cells have significant changes in metabolism (Best et al., 2018; DeNicola et al., 2015; DeNicola et al., 2011; Mitsuishi et al., 2012; Romero et al., 2017; Sayin et al., 2017), yet tumors derived from cells of these genotypes do not show significant alterations in levels of nutrients whose metabolism is known to be altered by Keap1 loss. Thus, differences in metabolite concentrations between TIF and plasma cannot be used to extrapolate consumption and release of metabolites by tumors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Keap1 loss experiment and supported by citations to Best et al., 2018; DeNicola et al., 2015; DeNicola et al., 2011; Mitsuishi et al., 2012; Romero et al., 2017; Sayin et al., 2017.

claim: PDAC tumor interstitial fluid is depleted of some nutrients relative to plasma.
source: First, we find PDAC tumor interstitial fluid is depleted of some nutrients relative to plasma.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: Depleted nutrients in PDAC TIF are not necessarily metabolites predicted to be depleted by cell culture studies.
source: Interestingly, these depleted nutrients are not necessarily metabolites predicted to be depleted by cell culture studies.
evidence: This is an observation comparing in vivo findings to cell culture predictions.

claim: PDAC cells consume large amounts of glucose and glutamine in culture.
source: For example, PDAC cells consume large amounts of glucose and glutamine in culture (Son et al., 2013; Ying et al., 2012), and it has been assumed that these nutrients are depleted in the microenvironment (Commisso et al., 2013; Kamphorst et al., 2015; Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017; Sherman et al., 2017; Sousa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Son et al., 2013; Ying et al., 2012; Commisso et al., 2013; Kamphorst et al., 2015; Lyssiotis and Kimmelman, 2017; Sherman et al., 2017; Sousa et al., 2016.

claim: Branched chain amino acids are proposed to be limiting for proliferation of PDAC cells in tumors.
source: Branched chain amino acids are also proposed to be limiting for proliferation of PDAC cells in tumors, requiring cancer cells to acquire those nutrients from alternative sources such as stromal cells or extracellular protein (Grankvist et al., 2018; Palm et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grankvist et al., 2018; Palm et al., 2015.

claim: Neither glutamine nor branched-chain amino acids are substantially depleted in PDAC tumors regardless of anatomical site.
source: We find that neither glutamine nor branched-chain amino acids are substantially depleted in PDAC tumors regardless of anatomical site.
evidence: This is a finding from the metabolite measurements.

claim: While glucose is depleted in PDAC TIF relative to circulatory levels, it is still present at millimolar concentration.
source: Further, while glucose is depleted in PDAC TIF relative to circulatory levels, it is still present at millimolar concentration, and glucose deprivation in TIF is not a universal feature of tumors (Siska et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the metabolite measurements and supported by a citation to Siska et al., 2017.

claim: The nutrient most strongly depleted from PDAC TIF is arginine.
source: We find that the nutrient most strongly depleted from PDAC TIF is arginine.
evidence: This is a finding from the metabolite measurements.

claim: Many cell types can synthesize arginine using urea cycle enzymes.
source: Many cell types can synthesize arginine using urea cycle enzymes (Wu et al., 2009), but these metabolic enzymes are silenced by many tumors to enhance nucleotide production (Rabinovich et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2009 and Rabinovich et al., 2015.

claim: PDAC tumors do not exhibit urea cycle enzyme silencing.
source: However, PDAC tumors do not exhibit urea cycle enzyme silencing (Lee et al., 2018; Uhlén et al., 2015) and are reported to have a functional urea cycle (Zaytouni et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2018; Uhlén et al., 2015; Zaytouni et al., 2017.

claim: PDAC cells may retain the urea cycle pathway to adapt to a tumor microenvironment with limited arginine availability.
source: Perhaps, PDAC cells retain this metabolic pathway to adapt to a tumor microenvironment with limited arginine availability.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: PDAC cells utilize macropinocytosis of environmental protein.
source: Additionally, PDAC cells utilize macropinocytosis of environmental protein (Commisso et al., 2013; Kamphorst et al., 2015), and this route of nutrient acquisition may allow PDAC cells to acquire sufficient arginine to support survival and growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Commisso et al., 2013; Kamphorst et al., 2015, and the speculation is an inference.

claim: TIF composition can alter the function of non-cancer cells, such as immune cells, in the tumor microenvironment.
source: TIF composition can alter the function of non-cancer cells, such as immune cells, in the tumor microenvironment (Buck et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Buck et al., 2017.

claim: PDAC tumors are highly immunosuppressive.
source: In contrast, PDAC tumors are highly immunosuppressive (Martinez-Bosch et al., 2018) and immunotherapy shows limited efficacy in this disease (Hilmi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martinez-Bosch et al., 2018 and Hilmi et al., 2018.

claim: Nutrient deprivation in PDAC TIF could contribute to PDAC immunosuppression.
source: Nutrient deprivation in PDAC TIF could contribute to PDAC immunosuppression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Both arginine and tryptophan are required for T cell function.
source: Both arginine and tryptophan, which are depleted in the autochthonous PDAC environment, are required for T cell function (Geiger et al., 2016; Moffett and Namboodiri, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Geiger et al., 2016; Moffett and Namboodiri, 2003.

claim: Depletion of myeloid cells capable of degrading arginine and tryptophan from PDAC tumors resulted in increased T cell infiltration, proliferation, and activation in PDAC tumors.
source: Intriguingly, depletion of myeloid cells capable of degrading arginine and tryptophan from PDAC tumors resulted in increased T cell infiltration, proliferation, and activation in PDAC tumors (Bayne et al., 2012; Stromnes et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bayne et al., 2012; Stromnes et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2017.

claim: Growing cancer cells in media with different nutrient compositions alters their metabolic requirements and response to drugs.
source: Indeed, growing cancer cells in media with different nutrient compositions alters their metabolic requirements and response to drugs (Cantor et al., 2017; Muir et al., 2017; Palm et al., 2015; Schug et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cantor et al., 2017; Muir et al., 2017; Palm et al., 2015; Schug et al., 2015.

claim: Ex vivo culture models using non-physiological nutrient levels have limited ability to identify tumor-essential metabolic genes.
source: That metabolism is responsive to environment may underpin the limited ability of ex vivo culture models using non-physiological nutrient levels to identify tumor-essential metabolic genes (Horvath et al., 2016; Muir and Vander Heiden, 2018; Ryan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horvath et al., 2016; Muir and Vander Heiden, 2018; Ryan et al., 2018.

claim: By characterizing the polar small molecule nutrients in PDAC and LUAD tumors, media that better approximates the nutrients available to cancer cells in tumors can be formulated.
source: By characterizing the polar small molecule nutrients in PDAC and LUAD tumors, media that better approximates the nutrients available to cancer cells in tumors can be formulated.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the findings.

claim: All experiments performed in this study were approved by the MIT Committee on Animal Care (IACUC).
source: All experiments performed in this study were approved by the MIT Committee on Animal Care (IACUC).
evidence: This is a statement of ethical compliance.

claim: All mice in this study were fully backcrossed to the C57BL/6J background.
source: All mice in this study were fully backcrossed to the C57BL/6J background.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Animals were housed on a 12 hr light and 12 hr dark cycle, with ad libitum access to food and water.
source: Animals were housed on a 12 hr light and 12 hr dark cycle, with ad libitum access to food and water.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: KP-/-C mice form end-stage tumors approximately 8–10 weeks after birth.
source: For studies using KrasG12D Trp53fl/fl Pdx-1-cre (KP-/-C) mice (Bardeesy et al., 2006), male and female animals of this genotype were allowed for form end-stage tumors, which occurred approximately 8–10 weeks after birth (Danai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by citations to Bardeesy et al., 2006 and Danai et al., 2018.

claim: 5–180 µL of TIF was able to be isolated from ~75% (13/17 tumors) of isolated KP-/-C PDAC tumors.
source: 5–180 µL of TIF was able to be isolated from ~75% (13/17 tumors) of isolated KP-/-C PDAC tumors.
evidence: This is a methodological observation.

claim: The amount of fluid collected per tumor weight is consistent with previous reports of TIF isolation from human tumor samples.
source: The amount of fluid collected per tumor weight is consistent with previous reports of TIF isolation from human tumor samples (Haslene-Hox et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haslene-Hox et al., 2011.
